opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of reasons. One is just the practical side of things. Pre-training is extremely expensive. If you want to train a competitive base model from scratch, you need thousands of GPUs, trillions of tokens, and a lot of engineering infrastructure. That's really only feasible for a handful of large companies. Post-training, on the other hand, is something where you can actually run meaningful experiments with a much more modest budget. You can take an open-weight base model and try different fine-tuning strategies, preference tuning, reinforcement learning approaches, and see real differences on a single node or even a single GPU in some cases.

The second reason is that I think we're seeing a lot of the recent capability gains coming from post-training rather than from scaling up pre-training alone. If you look at the reasoning models, for example, a lot of what makes them good at math and coding is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards applied on top of a base model that already had the knowledge, in a sense. The pre-training gives you this broad foundation, but post-training is where you shape the behavior, where you unlock certain capabilities and make the model actually useful. So there's still a lot of low-hanging fruit there, I would say.

And then there's also the observation that pre-training seems to be hitting some diminishing returns. We're running out of high-quality data on the internet, and simply making models bigger gets very costly for relatively incremental improvements. So the field is shifting toward asking, given a good base model, how do we get the most out of it? That includes things like better reward modeling, better RL algorithms, like the variations on PPO and GRPO, and also inference-time scaling, letting the model think longer.

So for researchers, and especially for people outside the big labs, I think post-training is where you can make a real contribution right now. It's more accessible, the iteration cycles are faster, and the impact on the final model quality is quite substantial.

r001.rationale: The response describes post-training as accessible, impactful, and a source of low-hanging fruit, but does not attribute those gains to the paradigm’s relative novelty.

r002.rationale: It gives reasoning models as an example of post-training gains, but does not identify reasoning as the main locus of current developments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main reason is that pre-training has become, in a sense, a solved problem — or at least a well-understood one. We know the recipe: you take a big transformer, you scale up the data, you scale up the compute, and you get a better base model. The improvements there are still happening, but they're incremental, and honestly, they're mostly out of reach for anyone who isn't at one of the big labs. If you don't have thousands of GPUs, you're not going to meaningfully move the needle on pre-training.

Post-training is different. That's where a lot of the interesting behavior actually comes from. The base model is essentially a very sophisticated next-token predictor, but what makes a model useful — following instructions, reasoning through a math problem, knowing when to say it doesn't know something — that's largely shaped in post-training. Supervised fine-tuning, preference tuning with something like DPO or RLHF, and now especially reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for reasoning models. If you look at what happened with DeepSeek-R1, the base model wasn't fundamentally new. What was new was how they applied RL on top of it to get those long chain-of-thought reasoning behaviors.

And the other thing I like about post-training is that it's accessible. You can do meaningful experiments on a single GPU, or even a handful of them, with open-weight models. You can take Llama or Qwen, run a fine-tuning or RL experiment, and actually learn something about what works. That makes it a much more productive area for researchers, for students, for people in industry who want to adapt models to their own domain. So it's both where the most interesting open questions are right now, and where the barrier to entry is low enough that a lot of people can contribute.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training is accessible and offers interesting opportunities, but does not attribute readily available performance gains to the research paradigm being relatively novel.

r002.rationale: It highlights reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for reasoning models as an especially important current development and cites DeepSeek-R1’s reasoning behavior as an example.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how much room there is to experiment, and who can actually do those experiments. With pretraining, you’re typically talking about enormous datasets and a substantial compute budget. If you want to study something at that scale, the barrier to entry is very high.

With post-training, you can start from an existing pretrained model and explore how to make better use of the capabilities it already has. How do you get it to follow instructions more reliably? How do you improve its reasoning? What kind of feedback is useful, and how do you turn that feedback into a better training signal? There are a lot of interesting research questions there, and many of them are accessible with much smaller budgets.

I wouldn’t say pretraining is solved or no longer important. But post-training gives you a relatively direct way to connect a research idea to a change in behavior that people actually care about. That combination of accessibility and potential impact makes it a particularly exciting area to work on.

r001.rationale: The response links post-training’s promise to accessibility, room for experimentation, and potential impact, but does not attribute readily available performance gains to the paradigm’s relative novelty.

r002.rationale: Reasoning is mentioned as one of several possible research questions, but the response does not identify it as the main locus of current post-training developments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one reason is that pretraining has become very resource intensive. If you want to study it at a meaningful scale, you need a lot of compute and a lot of data, which makes it difficult for smaller research groups to participate. And even if you run an experiment, getting feedback can take a long time.

With post-training, you can start from an existing pretrained model and ask, how do we make this model more useful? How do we improve its instruction following, or its ability to reason through a problem? You can do a lot of interesting work there with a much smaller compute budget, and the experiments are usually faster.

That doesn’t mean pretraining is solved. But I think post-training gives researchers more opportunities to try ideas and understand what actually makes a difference. You’re taking capabilities that the model already has and figuring out how to bring them out more reliably, and sometimes teaching it new behaviors. That’s a very interesting research space.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training offers accessible research opportunities, but does not attribute its performance gains to the paradigm’s relative novelty.

r002.rationale: It mentions improving reasoning alongside instruction following, but does not identify reasoning as the main locus of interesting current developments.
